habitat: Solitary in any tall woodland and riverine forest, especially where there are plenty of tall, dead trees.
summary: A common resident. A large, long-billed woodpecker with barred underparts and a bold black malar streak and ear-patch. Only the top of the male’s crown is red, and the forehead is black. The female has a black crown. The call is a loud wickwickwick-wick-wick, and the male drums a far-carrying trrrrrr-tap-tap-tap-tap-tap on a hollow branch. Newman lists it as Dendropicos namaquus. The scientific name here stays Chloropicus namaquus. The Kemp paper name Bearded Woodpecker and the code RB were left unchanged.

similar.note: Golden-tailed Woodpecker is streaked below and lacks the black ear-patch. Bearded Woodpecker is larger, with barred underparts.
Cardinal Woodpecker is much smaller, with a brown forehead and a streaked breast, not barred underparts and a black ear-patch.

tail.shape: Stiff. Newman’s family notes say it is used as a prop while feeding.

research.note: Newman calls it a common resident, and Avibase does not mark the Kruger occurrence rare or accidental, so status is resident and all twelve months are listed. Newman’s scientific name is Dendropicos namaquus. This file keeps Chloropicus namaquus. The immature was not described. Bill colour, eye, legs, wings and tail colour were not given. The front photograph is partly behind branches. No flight photograph was found. Drumming is stored as a male sound because Newman attributes it to the male. Population figures, the Kemp paper name Bearded Woodpecker and the code RB were left unchanged.
